meta.trim: lists over 60 items keep their first 60; objects over 120 keys keep their first 120; floats keep 6 significant digits

teaching.title: What kind of data this is
teaching.question: What kind of measurements are in this table?
teaching.one_liner: Pick all that apply. It changes what TurboTab checks and suggests, never what you can do.
teaching.why: Each field reads a table its own way: an assay has more columns than rows, a recall file repeats each person, a lab column can hold two units. A lens runs that field's checks and puts its usual choices first. It never hides a column, a model or an option.
teaching.consumer: The findings, the column roles and the order of every suggestion read it.

options.label: Dietary intake
options.consequence: Checks energy units and implausible intakes; offers energy adjustment and substitution curves.

options.label: Clinical measurements and labs
options.consequence: Separates impossible values from abnormal ones; checks units and censored results.

options.label: Metabolomics or proteomics
options.consequence: Looks for QC injections, run order, drift and values below detection.

options.label: Genomics or transcriptomics
options.consequence: Reads what the values are, counts or normalized, and plans for few samples.

options.label: Survey or questionnaire instruments
options.consequence: Finds shared response scales and codes outside them, such as 9 for no answer.

options.label: Something else, not sure
options.consequence: Runs the generic checks only; no field's defaults are applied, and the record says so.

terms.definition: A field's way of reading a table: which checks run and which choices are offered first. Several can apply at once.

sections.heading: Dietary intake
sections.body: Total energy is a strong determinant of every nutrient's intake, so adjusting for it changes what a nutrient's coefficient means: with energy fixed, more of one source is less of another (Tomova et al. 2022). Energy adjustment is the field's methodological signature. The dietary pack also checks energy units by the Atwater reconstruction (4·protein + 4·carbohydrate + 9·fat + 7·alcohol) and offers the implausible-intake screens.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#04 · Energy adjustment — the methodological signature

sections.heading: Clinical measurements and labs
sections.body: A reference interval holds the central 95% of healthy people by construction and is for annotation only. Plausibility bounds flag values no living patient could have. The two are different categories, and no generic outlier rule tells them apart; the bounds themselves are institution-specific.

evidence.source: research/CLINICAL_SURVEY_PACK.md#A1.2 · Reference ranges vs physiological plausibility

sections.heading: Metabolomics and proteomics
sections.body: Values below detection are usually filled with half the feature's minimum, the de-facto default. It is widely used and statistically criticized: it collapses every missing value to one point, deflating variance.

sections.heading: Genomics and transcriptomics
sections.body: With more features than samples, an unpenalized least-squares or logistic model is degenerate rather than merely overfit: infinitely many coefficient vectors fit the data exactly. Penalization, dimension reduction or one test per feature are the ways through; the elastic net is the standard choice if one model must be named.

sections.heading: Survey instruments
sections.body: Whether a Likert item is ordinal or interval is genuinely disputed. Run the other treatment as a sensitivity analysis; if the conclusion holds under both, the dispute is moot for your paper.

teaching.title: Which way round the table is
teaching.question: Which way round is this table?
teaching.one_liner: Assay exports come both ways; if the columns are samples, every check reads across the wrong axis.
teaching.why: In a table of samples, columns are analytes and differ by orders of magnitude while rows barely differ; here it reads the other way. A transposed table does not fail: it runs cleanly and means nothing. Turning it changes what a row is, so it is settled before anything is diagnosed or sealed.
teaching.consumer: The structural diagnosis, the findings, the outcome list and every later question read the turned table.

options.label: Rows are samples
options.consequence: The table stays as supplied; the record notes it was checked.

options.label: Rows are features
options.consequence: The table is turned: each sample becomes a row and each feature a column.

terms.definition: Features such as metabolites or genes in rows and samples in columns: the transpose of what modeling expects.
Turned around, so that the rows become columns and the columns become rows.

sections.heading: Exports come both ways
sections.body: Vendor exports from XCMS, MZmine, MS-DIAL and similar tools are overwhelmingly features in rows; MetaboAnalyst's own table is samples in rows. A tool must never guess silently: it presents the reading with its evidence and asks.

sections.heading: Genes in rows is the convention
sections.body: An expression matrix is stored with genes in rows and samples in columns, the inverse of what the rest of the app assumes. An undetected transpose does not error; it produces a PCA of genes labeled as samples.

teaching.title: Repairs before the outcome
teaching.question: Should this be repaired before anything is counted?
teaching.one_liner: A repair fixes how a value is written, row by row; it previews on your rows first and is recorded.
teaching.why: A sentinel code such as 9 on a 1–5 item is a missing answer, not a strong opinion; a value impossible in a living patient is an entry error. Repairs that look only at their own row run on the table now. Anything learned from many rows waits for the training folds.
teaching.consumer: The working table, the findings, the outcome list and every count downstream read the repaired values.

options.label: Apply the repair
options.consequence: The changed cells are written into the working table and listed in the record.

options.label: Ask me later
options.consequence: The finding waits inside the question it belongs to, checked and attributed.

options.label: Dismiss it
options.consequence: Nothing changes; the record keeps that it was seen and set aside.

terms.definition: A number standing for an answer that is not a value, such as 9 for don't know or 999 for not measured.
Computed from one row's own cells, so it leaks nothing about other rows and can run before the seal.

sections.heading: Sentinel codes
sections.body: In a 1–5 item, a 9 is not extremely agree; it is don't know or refused. Sentinels must be recoded, never automatically: some legitimate scales do run 0–9.

sections.heading: Impossible is not abnormal
sections.body: Plausibility bounds flag values no living patient could have; a reference interval holds the central 95% of healthy people and is for annotation only. The bounds themselves are institution-specific.

evidence.source: research/CLINICAL_SURVEY_PACK.md#A1.2 · Reference ranges vs physiological plausibility

sections.heading: Too many to count is a value
sections.body: TNTC, too numerous to count, means a plate held more colonies than its countable range, 15–300 per plate in FDA's Bacteriological Analytical Manual (2026 edition), which reads such a plate as a lower bound: the count is above that limit, right-censored like a result above the upper limit of quantitation, not missing. QNS, quantity not sufficient, and a hemolyzed specimen are measurement failures with no value: treat those as missing.

evidence.source: research/CLINICAL_SURVEY_PACK.md#A1.3 · Lab value formats and censored values

teaching.title: The outcome
teaching.question: Which column is the outcome you want to explain or predict?
teaching.one_liner: Everything downstream is built around it: who is counted, how rows are split, and what the models learn.
teaching.why: Rows without the outcome leave the analysis first, so the outcome sets the first count in the participant flow. It also decides the task, the metrics and which findings apply. When the outcome is itself energy-related, such as weight, BMI or diabetes, adjusting for reported energy needs extra care.
teaching.consumer: Task detection, the participant flow, the split and every model read it.

terms.definition: The column a model learns to predict or explain; also called the target or the dependent variable.
The count of rows at each step, from the file to the analysis, with the reason each step removed rows.

sections.heading: When the outcome is energy-related
sections.body: Total energy is plausibly on the causal path from diet composition to adiposity, and adiposity causes under-reporting of energy. Conditioning on reported energy can then be over-adjustment and collider bias at once. Present adjusted and unadjusted models and flag it as a limitation; the pack does not pick a side.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#04 · Energy adjustment — the methodological signature

sections.heading: Which N
sections.body: Report how many people each dietary exclusion removed, and why: STROBE-nut asks for the number excluded for missing, incomplete or implausible dietary data, and STROBE suggests a flow diagram, each box carrying an n and a reason. The outcome sets its first step.

teaching.title: The event
teaching.question: Which level of the outcome is the event?
teaching.one_liner: Models predict the event's probability; whether that is death or survival is your research question.
teaching.why: A two-level outcome needs one level coded 1, and nothing in the file says which: alive or dead has no correct default. The event fixes the meaning of every predicted probability, odds ratio and calibration curve, and the methods section names it.
teaching.consumer: The models, the sign of every coefficient, the calibration and each predicted probability read it.

terms.definition: The outcome level a binary model predicts the probability of, coded 1.
The outcome level coded 0; odds ratios compare the event against it.

sections.heading: Probabilities, not just ranks
sections.body: Judge models on calibration as well as discrimination: a well-calibrated model with a lower AUC can be more useful than a miscalibrated one with a higher AUC (Van Calster et al. 2019). Each fit here reports its calibration beside the AUC, the customary headline, and ranks the families on log loss, a strictly proper score that rewards calibrated probabilities.

sections.heading: A rare event is not a problem to resample away
sections.body: Undersampling, oversampling and SMOTE overestimate the probability of the minority class without improving discrimination. A rare event's real problem is small-sample overfitting, answered by penalization and sample size.

teaching.title: The kind of outcome
teaching.question: What kind of outcome is this column?
teaching.one_liner: The task decides which models apply and how they are scored.
teaching.why: A quantity is regression, scored by R², RMSE and MAE. Two classes are binary, scored by AUC, Brier score and log loss. Several unordered classes are multiclass. An ordered score, such as a 1–5 rating, is ordinal: regression would assume equal gaps, and classification would discard the order. An event whose follow-up varies is time to event.
teaching.consumer: The model shelf, the split's stratification and every metric read it.

options.label: Regression
options.consequence: The outcome is a quantity; models predict its value, ranked by the MSE, R² beside it.

options.label: Binary
options.consequence: Two classes; models predict the probability of one, ranked by log loss, AUC beside it.

options.label: Multiclass
options.consequence: Several unordered classes; models predict each class's probability, scored by log loss.

options.label: Ordinal
options.consequence: Ordered levels, such as a 1–5 rating; a proportional-odds model keeps their order.

options.label: Time to event
options.consequence: An event and each row's follow-up; Cox gives hazard ratios, ranked by a horizon's Brier score.

terms.definition: A model of a quantity: it predicts a number, and its errors are distances from the true value.
A model of classes: it predicts the probability that a row belongs to each one.
Classes with an order but no fixed spacing, such as a 1–5 rating; best modeled by a cumulative link model.

sections.heading: Ordered outcomes
sections.body: For an ordinal outcome, a cumulative link (proportional odds) model uses the full ordering and handles ties; a linear model on the score, or a split into responders and non-responders, does not.

sections.heading: Scores built from many items
sections.body: A multi-item scale score with many categories and no floor or ceiling is often analyzed as a quantity; whether that is safe is disputed. Run the other treatment as a sensitivity analysis.

teaching.title: How long people were followed
teaching.question: Was everyone followed for the same time, or could some leave first?
teaching.one_liner: If follow-up ends before the event for some people, a yes/no model counts them as having none.
teaching.why: In a cohort people enter at different times, move away, or the study ends before their event could happen. A yes/no model treats them as event-free and can manufacture an association; a time-to-event model keeps each person for the time they were followed (PROBAST, item 4.6).
teaching.consumer: The task, the model shelf (Cox for a time to event) and the methods read it.

options.label: Follow-up varies
options.consequence: Analyzed as a time to event: a Cox model, each row followed until its time.

options.label: Same for everyone
options.consequence: The yes/no outcome stands; the methods state that everyone was followed equally.

terms.definition: Follow-up that ends before the event could be seen: the person left, or the study ended.

sections.heading: Reporting follow-up
sections.body: Report median follow-up using the reverse Kaplan–Meier method, not the median of observed follow-up times, which is biased by early events.

teaching.title: Prediction or inference
teaching.question: Is this analysis for prediction or for inference?
teaching.one_liner: Prediction is judged on rows the model never saw; inference on estimates and their uncertainty.
teaching.why: The two lead to different models, different checks and a different methods section. Some advice even flips: a missing-value indicator is legitimate for prediction and biased for inference. Inference reports coefficients with confidence intervals; prediction reports performance on held-out rows and leaves coefficients uninterpreted.
teaching.consumer: The model shelf's order, the coefficient intervals and the Results read it.

options.label: Prediction
options.consequence: Models are ranked by performance on rows they never saw; coefficients are not interpreted.

options.label: Inference
options.consequence: Linear models report coefficients with confidence intervals; the shelf favors reportable models.

terms.definition: Estimating the outcome for new people as accurately as possible, judged on rows the model never saw.
Estimating how the outcome relates to an exposure, with the uncertainty of that estimate.
The exact quantity an analysis estimates, stated in words; two methods with different estimands answer different questions.

sections.heading: The advice that flips
sections.body: For prediction, a missing-value indicator is legitimate and often improves performance, because the same indicator is observable when the model is used. For inference in observational data it gives biased estimates (in a randomized trial it is valid for baseline covariates); multiple imputation, offered here, or a principled model of the missingness is required.

sections.heading: Hygiene for prediction
sections.body: Split by participant, not by row, and fit everything learned from data — energy-adjustment residuals, scaling, imputation — inside the training fold only.

teaching.title: Whether people repeat
teaching.question: Can one person appear in more than one row?
teaching.one_liner: You know this and the file only hints at it; the held-out rows cannot be drawn correctly without it.
teaching.why: If one person's rows land on both sides of the split, the model is scored on people it has already seen, and every score is inflated. A column that repeats is a suggestion, never the answer: the app checks your answer against the data and says so when they disagree.
teaching.consumer: The seal's grouping, the repeats and unit questions, and every cross-validation fold read it.

options.label: One row each
options.consequence: Each row is a different person; the split may draw rows freely.

options.label: People repeat
options.consequence: Rows sharing an identifier stay together; the next questions ask what repeats.

options.label: I don't know
options.consequence: Rows are held out one by one, and every held-out score is labeled exploratory.

terms.definition: A split that keeps all of one participant's rows on the same side, so repeat measurements cannot leak across.
What one row of the table is: one person, one visit, one recall or one sample.

sections.heading: Split by participant
sections.body: With repeated recalls, a row-level split puts one person's days on both sides and inflates every score. Split by participant, not by row.

sections.heading: What repeats can look like
sections.body: Duplicate participant identifiers mean repeated measures; look for the occasion too, such as a day, visit or recall number, or a date. Twin columns such as `DR1TKCAL` and `DR2TKCAL` are the same structure in wide form.

teaching.title: What repeats
teaching.question: Are these repeats or different time points?
teaching.one_liner: Replicates of one quantity can be averaged; time points carry change that averaging would erase.
teaching.why: Two recalls days apart measure one usual diet twice, so their mean reduces day-to-day error. Clinic visits months apart measure a person changing, so the order is the signal. Dates with no visit structure suggest repeats; a visit label or spaced dates suggest time points. Where the evidence is thin, this is asked.
teaching.consumer: The aggregation menu, its recommended default and the temporal question read it.

options.label: Repeats
options.consequence: Repeated measurements of one quantity, such as two recalls; averaging is offered first.

options.label: Time points
options.consequence: Different moments in time; averaging is not offered first, and order matters.

options.label: Imputed copies
options.consequence: Copies of one record from multiple imputation; under inference kept only as a recorded limitation.

terms.definition: A repeated measurement of the same quantity under the same conditions, such as a second recall of usual diet.
A measurement at a distinct moment, such as a visit, where change between moments is part of the data.

sections.heading: Why two recalls exist
sections.body: A single 24-hour recall measures one day, not usual diet. Two or more non-consecutive recalls separate day-to-day variation from real differences between people; with one recall that separation is impossible.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#03 · Repeated recalls and measurement error

sections.heading: Consecutive days are not independent
sections.body: Recalls on consecutive days have correlated errors, so within-person variation is underestimated and the data look more reliable than they are. NHANES uses non-consecutive days by design.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#03 · Repeated recalls and measurement error
research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#03 · Repeated recalls and measurement error

teaching.title: One row in the analysis
teaching.question: When you analyze this, what is one row?
teaching.one_liner: People appear more than once; that leaves two honest options, and they lead to different analyses.
teaching.why: One row per person combines each person's records, and the next question asks how. One row per record keeps them as they are, and the split keeps each person's records on one side. There is no default: guessing here is how the leak this check exists to prevent begins.
teaching.consumer: The aggregation question, the working table, the participant flow and the seal read it.

options.label: One row per person
options.consequence: Each person's records are combined into one row; the next question asks how.

options.label: One row per record
options.consequence: Records stay as they are; held-out people never appear in training.

terms.definition: A split that keeps all of one participant's rows on the same side, so repeat measurements cannot leak across.
What one row of the modeled table stands for: a person, or one of their records.

sections.heading: Leakage across a person's rows
sections.body: If a person contributes several recalls, rows from the same person must never be split across training and test folds; anything estimated from the data, such as a residual energy adjustment, is fit inside the training fold.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#03 · Repeated recalls and measurement error

teaching.title: Combining each person's rows
teaching.question: How should each person's rows be combined?
teaching.one_liner: The right summary depends on what repeats: averaging replicates reduces error, averaging time points destroys the signal.
teaching.why: For repeated recalls, the mean is an acceptable exposure for ranking people, still measured with error: alone it is attenuated toward zero, but beside other error-prone intakes it can be inflated or flip sign. For visits, choose the baseline, the last visit or the change. When the outcome itself varies within a person, say which value is the outcome.
teaching.consumer: The working table, the participant flow, the seal and every model read the combined rows.

options.label: Mean
options.consequence: Each person's rows are averaged; replicates' day-to-day error shrinks.

options.label: First (baseline)
options.consequence: Each person keeps their first row, such as the baseline visit.

options.label: Last
options.consequence: Each person keeps their most recent row.

options.label: Change from baseline
options.consequence: Each measurement becomes the last value minus the first: change over time.

terms.definition: The shrinking of a lone exposure's association toward zero because it is measured with error; averaging more days reduces it.
A person's long-run average intake, which single days only estimate; modeling it properly is more than a mean.

sections.heading: When the mean is adequate
sections.body: To rank people for regression, classification or a predictive model, the mean of the available recalls is an acceptable exposure and what most cohort analyses use. Under classical error it is attenuated toward zero only as the model's one error-prone exposure: with several error-prone nutrients, or energy, in the model, a coefficient can be attenuated, inflated or change sign (Keogh et al. 2020; Freedman et al. 2011).

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#03 · Repeated recalls and measurement error

sections.heading: When the mean is not adequate
sections.body: Prevalence or percentile claims about usual intake, episodically consumed foods with many zero days, and exposure coefficients that must be unbiased in magnitude all need more than a mean. This version corrects energy-adjusted exposure coefficients by regression calibration from the repeated recalls; it fits no usual-intake distribution.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#03 · Repeated recalls and measurement error

sections.heading: Cumulative averages over follow-up
sections.body: With repeated questionnaires, the cohort standard is the cumulative average up to each event; if diet changes because of preclinical disease, a lag is conventional.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#03 · Repeated recalls and measurement error
research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#03 · Repeated recalls and measurement error

teaching.title: Predicting forward in time
teaching.question: Are you predicting something later from measurements taken earlier?
teaching.one_liner: A random split is optimistic when the task looks forward; the held-out people should then be those seen last.
teaching.why: With visits kept as rows, a random split lets the model learn from a person's later visits and be scored on their earlier ones. Validation in time, holding out those seen last, is a distinct check from validation on random rows, and reporting guidelines treat it so.
teaching.consumer: The seal and the folds: ordered by time when yes, grouped by person either way.

options.label: Yes, later from earlier
options.consequence: Those seen last are held out whole, earlier visits included; folds run forward in time.

options.label: No
options.consequence: The held-out rows are drawn at random, each person's rows kept together.

terms.definition: A split that keeps all of one participant's rows on the same side, so repeat measurements cannot leak across.
A split that holds out the people seen last, whole, by their latest date; their earlier rows can predate training rows.

sections.heading: Split by participant
sections.body: Split by participant, not by row, and fit everything learned from data inside the training fold only.

sections.heading: Resample the whole pipeline
sections.body: Internal validation must resample the entire modeling pipeline: imputation, transformation, selection and tuning.

teaching.title: What each column is
teaching.question: What role does each column play in the analysis?
teaching.one_liner: Only exposures, covariates and the energy column can become predictors; every other role stays out of the models.
teaching.why: An identifier names a person and cannot generalize. Survey weights and design columns describe how people were sampled, and a flag such as `imputed_weight` describes how a value was filled. None of them measures the participant, so each stays out of the predictors while the record keeps it.
teaching.consumer: The participant flow, the split's grouping, energy adjustment and the model matrix read it.

options.label: Identifier
options.consequence: Names a participant; never a predictor, and keeps a person's rows together in the split.

options.label: Exposure
options.consequence: What you are studying; a predictor, and energy adjustment applies to its nutrients.

options.label: Energy
options.consequence: Total energy intake; energy adjustment is computed against it and decides whether it stays.

options.label: Covariate
options.consequence: Adjusted for, such as age or sex; enters the models beside the exposures.

options.label: Cluster
options.consequence: Groups participants, such as a site or household; kept out of the predictors.

options.label: Survey design
options.consequence: A survey weight, stratum or sampling unit; kept out of the predictors.

options.label: Flag
options.consequence: Marks another column's values, such as imputed ones; kept out of the predictors.

options.label: Time
options.consequence: When a row was measured, such as a cycle or visit; kept out of the predictors.

options.label: Excluded
options.consequence: Left out of the analysis; the record keeps the column and the reason.

terms.definition: The variable whose relationship with the outcome the study is about, such as a nutrient intake.
A variable adjusted for so that the exposure's estimate is not confounded by it, such as age or sex.
A column that names a row or a person rather than measuring anything; a value that appears once cannot generalize.

sections.heading: Survey design columns
sections.body: NHANES oversamples some age, race and income groups on purpose. Without its weights, means are biased toward the oversampled groups; without strata and PSUs, standard errors are too small. Dietary analyses use `WTDRD1` for day 1 or `WTDR2D` for both days, not the examination weight `WTMEC2YR`. Under inference the survey question then asks whether the estimates describe the surveyed population (weighted, with design-based intervals) or these participants.

sections.heading: Pooled cycles
sections.body: Combining NHANES cycles from 2001–2002 on means dividing the two-year weights by the number of cycles combined. 1999–2000 is the exception: its two-year weights and 2001–2002's rest on different censuses, so the 1999–2002 rows take the four-year weight, doubled, before the division (NHANES Analytic Guidelines 2011–2016 §3.1.3–3.1.4). Confirm the same dietary method applies across cycles.

sections.heading: Units decide everything downstream
sections.body: 1 kcal = 4.184 kJ, and a column ending `_pct_kcal` is a share of energy, not an amount. Every implausibility screen, energy adjustment and substitution is a function of total energy, so a unit error there reaches every result.

teaching.title: Groups above the person
teaching.question: Are participants grouped in sites, centres, households or batches?
teaching.one_liner: People in one group are more alike than people across groups, so the model and its intervals must know the groups.
teaching.why: Under inference a site that differs in both exposure and outcome confounds the estimate, and intervals that treat its participants as independent are too narrow: each site gets its own intercept and the intervals are clustered by it. Under prediction, validation keeps a group together and can hold out whole groups.
teaching.consumer: The model's intercepts, the intervals, the split's internal–external option and the methods read it.

options.label: Adjust and cluster
options.consequence: Each group gets its own intercept; intervals are cluster-robust by the group.

options.label: Cluster only
options.consequence: Intervals cluster-robust by the group; differences between groups stay in the estimate.

options.label: No grouping
options.consequence: Every participant is analyzed as independent; recorded with its reason.

terms.definition: One intercept per group, so the exposure is compared within groups, never between them.
Intervals that let rows in one group share more than chance; few groups need a small-sample correction.

sections.heading: Validation keeps a unit's rows together
sections.body: Predictive-modeling hygiene for this data type: split by participant, not by row; fit energy-adjustment residual models, PCA/RRR loadings, standardization, and imputation inside the training fold only.

teaching.title: Whose estimate it is
teaching.question: Should the estimates describe the surveyed population, or these participants?
teaching.one_liner: The population answer weights each row and takes intervals from the strata and PSUs; the other is unweighted, and says so.
teaching.why: A survey oversamples some groups on purpose, so an unweighted estimate describes the sample, not the population, and can even change sign. Rows sampled in the same PSU resemble each other, so intervals that ignore the design are too narrow. Restricting the analysis keeps every row in the design, as a domain.
teaching.consumer: The coefficient table, its intervals, the eligibility rows and the methods section read it.

options.label: Surveyed population
options.consequence: Weighted estimates with Taylor-linearized intervals over the strata and PSUs.

options.label: These participants
options.consequence: Unweighted; the methods state a sample-only estimand whose intervals ignore the design.

terms.definition: Primary sampling unit: the cluster, such as a county, drawn first; people from one PSU resemble each other.
The rows an analysis is about. The others stay in the survey design, so the variance still sees every stratum and PSU.
The design-based variance of an estimate, from how much the PSU totals of its scores vary within each stratum.
The exact quantity an analysis estimates, stated in words; two methods with different estimands answer different questions.

sections.heading: Why the design matters
sections.body: Without the weights, estimates are biased toward the oversampled groups; without strata and PSUs, standard errors are too small because clustering within PSUs is ignored. NCHS states that variance estimates computed under a simple-random-sample assumption are generally too low for NHANES.

sections.heading: Restrict by domain, never by deleting rows
sections.body: To restrict to a subgroup, keep every row and mark the subgroup (`subset()` on a `svydesign` object, `DOMAIN` in SAS). Deleting rows drops PSUs and strata from the variance and gives wrong standard errors. Degrees of freedom are the PSUs minus the strata that hold the subgroup (NHANES Analytic Guidelines 2011–2016 §3.2.3).

sections.heading: A stratum with one PSU
sections.body: Taylor linearization estimates a stratum's variance from the spread between its PSUs, and one PSU has none. TurboTab centers such a stratum at the mean of all PSU totals (R's lonely.psu "adjust", Stata's singleunit(centered)), which is conservative, and names the stratum.

teaching.title: Who the study is about
teaching.question: Is your study restricted to part of this data?
teaching.one_liner: A restriction comes from your research question, so the outcome's distribution is not shown here.
teaching.why: A criterion such as an age range changes N and is reported in the participant flow before any rows are sealed. A cut chosen by looking at the outcome is data-driven selection, its own bias. Implausible-intake screens are offered with the rows each removes; under-reporting concentrates in higher BMI, so many analyses keep everyone.
teaching.consumer: The participant flow, the seal and every model's rows read it.

options.label: Keep every row
options.consequence: No row is excluded; the record states that no exclusion was applied.

options.label: Willett 2013, by sex
options.consequence: Women outside 500–3,500 and men outside 800–4,000 kcal a day are excluded.

options.label: NHS/HPFS, by sex
options.consequence: Women outside 500–3,500 (NHS) and men outside 800–4,200 (HPFS) kcal a day are excluded.

options.label: 500–5,000 kcal a day
options.consequence: Anyone outside 500–5,000 kcal a day is excluded, whatever their sex.

options.label: 500–3,500 kcal a day
options.consequence: Anyone outside 500–3,500 kcal a day is excluded; stricter, so it removes more.

options.label: Goldberg, energy over BMR
options.consequence: Energy over estimated BMR outside the cut-offs for a stated PAL and recall days is excluded.

options.label: Your own range
options.consequence: Rows outside a range you set on a numeric column, never the outcome, are excluded.

terms.definition: Who the study is about, such as an age range: applied to every row before the seal and reported with its count.
A reported day's energy intake too low or too high to be a real diet, usually a reporting error.
Reporting less than was eaten. It is systematic, concentrated in people with higher BMI and in weight-conscious participants.
A screen comparing reported energy with estimated basal metabolic rate, within limits that widen as recall days fall; widely used, and chosen by research purpose.

sections.heading: Each criterion its own box
sections.body: Track the rows through every filter, each eligibility criterion separately, with its reason and its count. A single excluded box tells a reader nothing about who is missing from the model's population.

sections.heading: The screens in circulation
sections.body: Willett's textbook (2013) gives 500–3,500 kcal a day for women and 800–4,000 for men. The Nurses' Health Study (women) and the Health Professionals Follow-up Study (men) use 500–3,500 and 800–4,200. Variants use 5,000 as men's upper bound, or a sex-neutral 500–5,000 or 500–3,500. The conventions genuinely differ across literatures, so show how N moves with the choice.

sections.heading: What exclusion does not fix
sections.body: In one simulation built on a biomarker study, Goldberg cut-offs reduced but did not remove bias in 14 of 24 nutrient–outcome associations and did not reduce it in the other 10; fixed kcal screens were not evaluated (Yamamoto et al. 2023). Whether to exclude at all is disputed: decide by the research purpose, not a general rule.

sections.heading: A common default
sections.body: Drop only unreliable recalls and impossible values, run the primary analysis on the full sample with energy adjustment, and present the misreporter-excluded analysis as a prespecified sensitivity analysis. A reviewer in an obesity journal may expect exclusion.

sections.heading: Who is excluded
sections.body: Under-reporting is concentrated in people with higher BMI, so excluding under-reporters when the outcome is adiposity removes a non-random slice of exactly the population studied. Report the excluded group's characteristics.

teaching.title: Missing predictor values
teaching.question: How should rows with missing predictor values be handled?
teaching.one_liner: The answer depends on the purpose: inference imputes with the outcome, prediction without it.
teaching.why: Complete cases keep only rows with every predictor measured, which can remove a large, non-random share. Under inference, multiple imputation fills each blank many times from the other variables, the outcome included, and pools the answers. Under prediction, a fill learned in each training fold without the outcome lets the model impute a new row the same way.
teaching.consumer: The participant flow, each model's pipeline and the banner's row counts read it.

options.label: Multiple imputation
options.consequence: Under inference: each blank imputed 20 times with the outcome; results pooled by Rubin's rules.

options.label: Complete cases
options.consequence: Rows missing any predictor are dropped; the participant flow shows how many.

options.label: Fill in each fold
options.consequence: Under prediction: blanks filled in each training fold without the outcome; every row stays.

terms.definition: Analyzing only rows with every variable measured; it can bias estimates when who is missing depends on the outcome.
Filling each blank several times from its predicted distribution, analyzing each copy and pooling the results by Rubin's rules.
Filling a missing value with an estimate learned from observed rows; a single fill understates the uncertainty.
Missingness that the observed columns explain; the assumption standard multiple imputation relies on.

sections.heading: One rule, by purpose
sections.body: The outcome's place in the imputation model depends on the purpose. Under inference, missing predictors are multiply imputed with the outcome and total energy in the imputation model, and the analyses pooled by Rubin's rules (Moons et al. 2006, via Harrell). Under prediction, they are imputed inside each training fold without the outcome, so the fitted pipeline can impute a new row as it was developed (Sisk et al. 2023).

sections.heading: Blanks often mean something
sections.body: On a food-frequency questionnaire a blank frequently means never, especially among older participants. That missingness is not at random, and standard multiple imputation assumes it is: an improvement, not a solution.

sections.heading: A zero is not a blank
sections.body: A zero on a 24-hour recall is a zero for that day, not a person who never eats the food.

sections.heading: Filling with the mean or median
sections.body: For inference, mean or median filling understates variance and biases coefficients; the clinical pack calls it indefensible in a manuscript, and here it is blocked until recorded. For prediction, a fill learned in each training fold is the deployable choice.

sections.heading: Values below detection
sections.body: A blank below a detection limit is small, not unknown: the median puts it in the middle of the distribution. Half the minimum is customary; a censoring-aware fill is sound for associations.

teaching.title: The seal: held-out rows
teaching.question: How many rows should be sealed for one final, untouched score?
teaching.one_liner: Sealed rows are scored once, when you open the seal at the end; every choice is tuned by cross-validation on the rest.
teaching.why: A model scored on the rows it was tuned on grades its own homework. The seal states its basis: grouped by an identifier, repeats found but not grouped, or undetermined, which is labeled exploratory. A small holdout measures little, so with few rows cross-validation alone comes first.
teaching.consumer: The participant flow, every model's cross-validation and the held-out score read it.

options.label: Cross-validation only
options.consequence: No rows are sealed; every score comes from cross-validation on all rows.

options.label: Hold out 10%
options.consequence: One row in ten is sealed for the final score; more rows train.

options.label: Hold out 20%
options.consequence: One row in five is sealed for the final score.

options.label: Hold out 30%
options.consequence: Nearly a third is sealed: a steadier final score, fewer rows to train.

terms.definition: Rows set aside before any modeling and scored once, at the end; the closest thing to new data you have.
The line between the held-out rows and the rest: drawn before modeling, opened once, its basis stated.
Splitting the training rows into folds, fitting on all but one and scoring on the one left out, in turn.
One of the equal parts cross-validation splits the training rows into; each is scored by a model that never saw it.
A split that keeps all of one participant's rows on the same side, so repeat measurements cannot leak across.
The number that fixes the random draw, so the same split can be drawn again.
How much better a model scores on the rows it learned from than on new rows; the bootstrap estimates it, refitting everything, and subtracts it.
Cross-validation drawn again on fresh folds and averaged, so the score rests on no single partition.
Each site, study or period held out in turn and scored by models fit on the others, showing how performance varies.

sections.heading: Split by participant
sections.body: With repeated recalls, a row-level split puts one person's days on both sides and inflates every score. Split by participant, not by row.

sections.heading: Everything learned stays inside the fold
sections.body: Everything supervised — feature ranking, selection, thresholds, tuning — happens inside the training fold. Selecting features on all samples can report near-zero error when no signal exists at all.

sections.heading: Resample the whole pipeline
sections.body: Internal validation must resample the entire modeling pipeline: imputation, transformation, selection and tuning.

sections.heading: A single split is the weakest
sections.body: Bootstrap optimism correction is the recommended default and repeated cross-validation is acceptable; a single train and test split is the weakest option at typical clinical sample sizes.

sections.heading: How precise the scores are here
sections.body: Each cross-validated score carries its standard error, and each pair of families an interval for their difference, computed on these rows. Read whether two models differ from that interval, not from a rule about sample size.

teaching.title: The exposure and its effect
teaching.question: Which exposure, and which of its effects, does this analysis estimate?
teaching.one_liner: Inference reports one declared effect; no estimate is shown until it is named.
teaching.why: A coefficient answers a question only once the question is fixed: which exposure, its total or its direct effect, a substitution or an addition of calories, and on which scale. Choosing these after seeing the estimates is a forking path. Only the measures TurboTab fits are offered.
teaching.consumer: The adjustment set, the energy model, the caption of every estimate and the methods read it.

options.label: Total effect
options.consequence: Everything the exposure changes downstream counts; mediators stay out of the model.

options.label: Direct effect
options.consequence: Mediators are held fixed; their confounders must be adjusted for too.

terms.definition: The exact quantity an analysis estimates, stated in words; two methods with different estimands answer different questions.
An odds or hazard ratio changes when a covariate that predicts the outcome is added, even without confounding.

sections.heading: A substitution, not an addition
sections.body: An energy-adjusted coefficient is a substitution estimate. It answers 'what if this person got more of their calories from X and correspondingly fewer from everything else, at the same total intake?' — not 'what if this person ate more X?'

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#04 · Energy adjustment — the methodological signature

teaching.title: The adjustment set
teaching.question: For each covariate: what causes what, and when was it measured?
teaching.one_liner: Each covariate's role is derived from your answers; covariates sharing a guess are confirmed together.
teaching.why: Statistics cannot tell a confounder from a mediator; only what causes what can (VanderWeele 2019). So the disjunctive cause criterion is asked: adjust for causes of the exposure or the outcome, leave out instruments and what the exposure changed, and estimate a covariate of unknown timing with and without it.
teaching.consumer: Which columns enter the model, the declared secondary model and the caption read it.

options.label: Confounder
options.consequence: A cause of the exposure and the outcome: adjusted for.

options.label: Mediator
options.consequence: Changed by the exposure and a cause of the outcome: left out of a total effect.

options.label: Timing unknown
options.consequence: Estimated without it and, declared beside, with it.

terms.definition: A variable on the path from the exposure to the outcome; adjusting for it removes part of the effect.
A consequence of two variables; adjusting for it can create an association between them that is not causal.
A cause of the exposure that affects the outcome only through it; adjusting for it amplifies any confounding left.

sections.heading: When energy or body size may be a mediator
sections.body: Your outcome is BMI/adiposity. Total energy is plausibly on the causal pathway from diet composition to adiposity, and adiposity causes under-reporting of energy. Conditioning on reported total energy here can be simultaneously over-adjustment (mediator) and collider-stratification bias. Present both adjusted and unadjusted models, and flag this in limitations.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#04 · Energy adjustment — the methodological signature

teaching.title: An exposure that changes over time
teaching.question: How is an exposure that changes over time estimated?
teaching.one_liner: A confounder that earlier exposure changed needs g-methods; their diagnostics come before any estimate.
teaching.why: When a confounder of later exposure was itself changed by earlier exposure, standard regression is biased either way: adjusting for it removes part of the effect, and leaving it out leaves later exposure confounded (Robins, Hernán & Brumback 2000). Weights or simulation adjust for it at each time point.
teaching.consumer: The weights, the outcome model, the simulated risks and the methods read it.

options.label: Marginal structural model
options.consequence: Weights balance the confounders at each time point; their distribution is read first.

options.label: Parametric g-formula
options.consequence: Simulates the confounders forward under always and never exposed, and compares the risks.

options.label: Standard regression
options.consequence: Sound only when no confounder was changed by earlier exposure; otherwise recorded as biased.

terms.definition: A covariate measured at each time point that affects later exposure and the outcome; earlier exposure may change it.
The probability of a unit's exposure history given its baseline covariates, over that given its confounders too; the mean should be near 1.
At each time point some units are exposed and some are not, so the effect comes from the data rather than the model alone.

sections.heading: Exposure updated over follow-up, and reverse causation
sections.body: With repeated FFQs across follow-up, the standard cohort approach is the cumulative average — averaging all FFQs up to each event time — which reduces within-person error relative to baseline-only. Caveat: if exposure changes because of preclinical disease, cumulative averaging imports reverse causation, so a lag or a stop-updating-at-diagnosis rule is conventional.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#03 · Repeated recalls and measurement error

teaching.title: Energy adjustment
teaching.question: How should nutrient intakes be adjusted for total energy?
teaching.one_liner: People who eat more eat more of everything; each method answers a different question about a nutrient.
teaching.why: Total energy drives every nutrient's intake, and the errors in reported nutrients and energy move together. Adjusting for it changes the question: the standard model and the residual method with energy kept swap calories between sources at fixed total energy; partition adds calories; all components gives each source's added and average swapped calories. Choose by the question.
teaching.consumer: Each model's pipeline, the column lineage, the coefficients and the substitution curves read it.

options.label: No adjustment
options.consequence: Total energy leaves the model: absolute intake, mixed with how much people eat.

options.label: Standard model
options.consequence: Energy stays in the model: more of the nutrient in place of other calories.

options.label: Residual, energy kept
options.consequence: Each nutrient's residual on energy, energy kept: the standard model's swap, in its units.

options.label: Residual, energy dropped
options.consequence: Each nutrient's residual on energy, energy dropped: differs when covariates track energy.

options.label: Density plus energy
options.consequence: Nutrient per calorie, energy its own term: obscure, and still biased (Tomova 2022).

options.label: Density alone
options.consequence: Nutrient per calorie, energy dropped: a rescaled effect whose meaning is obscure.

options.label: Energy partition
options.consequence: Calories from the nutrient and from everything else: adding calories, not substituting.

options.label: All components
options.consequence: Every energy source its own term: added calories, and each one's average swap.

terms.definition: The exact quantity an analysis estimates, stated in words; two methods with different estimands answer different questions.
Replacing a nutrient by its residual from a regression on total energy, re-centered at its mean, so it no longer tracks energy.
More of one energy source in place of others at the same total energy; what an energy-adjusted coefficient describes.
A nutrient's amount per unit of energy, such as grams per 1,000 kcal.
Splitting total energy into calories from the nutrient and calories from everything else, each its own term.
A partition with every energy source its own term; a source's average swap is its coefficient less the others', weighted by their share of energy.
An energy source not in the model; total energy carries it in one composite, so every swap is partly in its place.
Part of another column's total, such as `fat_sat` within `fat_total`: a partition would count it twice, and a substitution moves it with its total.

sections.heading: Why adjust at all
sections.body: Total energy drives nutrient intake through body size, activity and reporting scale; the hypothesis is usually about composition, not quantity; and correlated reporting errors in nutrients and energy partly cancel once energy is accounted for.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#04 · Energy adjustment — the methodological signature

sections.heading: Residual and standard: when they agree
sections.body: With total energy also in the model, swapping a nutrient for its residual only reparametrizes it, so the coefficient, its interval and p are identical to the standard model's, covariates or not; that is the residual method here unless you choose to drop energy (McCullough & Byrd 2023). With energy dropped, the coefficient is the standard model's only when no covariate correlates with energy, and its interval is wider even then; otherwise it differs, sometimes in sign.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#04 · Energy adjustment — the methodological signature

sections.heading: What the coefficient means
sections.body: An energy-adjusted coefficient is a substitution estimate: more of this nutrient and correspondingly less of everything else, at the same total intake — not the effect of simply eating more of it. With several energy sources in the model, "everything else" is only the sources left out of it; name them.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#04 · Energy adjustment — the methodological signature

sections.heading: All components
sections.body: Every energy source its own term in kcal: each coefficient is the total effect of adding that source's calories, and its average swap is the coefficient less the other sources', weighted by their share of the remaining energy (Tomova et al. 2022). It avoids composite variable bias at a cost in precision, one term per source, and its use is disputed (Willett, Stampfer & Tobias 2022).

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#04 · Energy adjustment — the methodological signature

sections.heading: The biases they share
sections.body: Standard and residual models are biased even without confounding (composite variable bias), and all four models only partly account for confounding by common dietary causes; each evaluates a different estimand (Tomova et al. 2022, AJCN). The density model's coefficient is an obscure quantity, and with energy added as a term it is more accurate but still biased; the all-components model is the paper's recommended route.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#04 · Energy adjustment — the methodological signature

sections.heading: The field's default
sections.body: The Willett residual method, computed within the final analytic sample and within sex, on log-transformed intakes, with the predicted nutrient at the mean energy added back. It is the field default, but not uncontested. Here total energy stays in the outcome model beside it unless you choose the energy-dropped form.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#04 · Energy adjustment — the methodological signature

sections.heading: When the outcome is BMI or adiposity
sections.body: Energy may be on the causal path and a collider at once. Present adjusted and unadjusted models and flag it in the limitations; the pack does not pick a side. An outcome named as weight, BMI, waist, body fat or diabetes raises this on the card.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#04 · Energy adjustment — the methodological signature

sections.heading: Fit inside the folds
sections.body: The nutrient-on-energy regression is learned from data, so it is fit on training rows only; fitting it on all rows before cross-validation leaks the held-out rows into every fold.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#04 · Energy adjustment — the methodological signature

teaching.title: Causal machine learning
teaching.question: Also estimate the effect with flexible learners and cross-fitting?
teaching.one_liner: DML and TMLE estimate the declared effect without assuming the outcome model's form; the assumptions come first.
teaching.why: A regression's estimate is right only if its form is. Double machine learning and targeted maximum likelihood learn the outcome and the exposure flexibly, cross-fitted so the intervals stay valid. They still rest on no unmeasured confounding, positivity, consistency and time ordering, so each is declared before any estimate.
teaching.consumer: The causal estimate, its diagnostics, the methods sentence and the plan lock read it.

options.label: Double ML, partially linear
options.consequence: A numeric exposure's effect per unit, every nuisance model cross-fitted.

options.label: Double ML, interactive
options.consequence: A yes/no exposure's average effect, or its effect among the exposed.

options.label: Targeted maximum likelihood
options.consequence: A yes/no exposure's average effect, doubly robust, inside the outcome's range.

options.label: Post-double-selection lasso
options.consequence: Two lassos choose among many declared candidates; the intervals stay valid.

options.label: The primary model only
options.consequence: No causal machine-learning estimate beside the primary model.

terms.definition: Each row's nuisance predictions come from models fit on the other folds, so its own noise never fits itself.
Every kind of participant could have had either exposure level; without it the estimate extrapolates.
Consistent when either the outcome model or the propensity model is right.

sections.heading: The learners adjust; your answers identify
sections.body: Penalized regression is a remedy for collinearity, not a source of causal identification. The lasso and the learners choose only among the covariates your answers adjust for; the identification comes from that set and the assumptions you declare.

sections.heading: Survey weights: say which estimate it is
sections.body: With survey weights, decide explicitly whether the estimate generalizes to the surveyed population (weights in every fit, a design-based variance) or describes these participants (unweighted, and said so).

teaching.title: Model families
teaching.question: Which model families should be fit and compared?
teaching.one_liner: Each family brings its own assumptions about how nutrients relate to the outcome; fitting several shows what depends on them.
teaching.why: A linear model assumes straight-line, additive effects and gives coefficients you can report. An elastic net shrinks correlated nutrients together, which suits diets where nutrients travel in foods. Boosted trees find curves and interactions but give no coefficients. In one comparison of 30,000 models, the algorithm mattered less than the endpoint and the analyst.
teaching.consumer: The fit, the Results and the substitution curves read it.

options.label: Linear model
options.consequence: OLS or logistic regression: one reportable coefficient per predictor, with intervals for inference.

options.label: Elastic net
options.consequence: A penalized linear model: shrinks correlated nutrients together, tuned inside training folds.

options.label: Boosted trees
options.consequence: Many shallow trees: finds curves and interactions; gives no coefficients.

options.label: Feature-wise tests
options.consequence: Tests each exposure on its own, adjusted for the covariates, with Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery control; no predictions.

options.label: Screened elastic net
options.consequence: Keeps the features most tied to the outcome in each training fold, then an elastic net.

options.label: Proportional-odds model
options.consequence: Cumulative odds ratios for an ordered outcome, the same at every cut-point; Brant's test checks it.

options.label: Mixed model
options.consequence: A random intercept per unit: model-based intervals when rows repeat, even within few units.

options.label: GEE
options.consequence: Population-average effects, with intervals robust to how a unit's repeated rows correlate.

options.label: Cox model
options.consequence: Hazard ratios for a time-to-event outcome, using every row's follow-up, censored or not.

terms.definition: What a model assumes before it sees data, such as straight lines or interactions; it decides what the model can find.
Shrinking coefficients toward zero to trade a little bias for less variance; essential when predictors are many or correlated.
Whether predicted probabilities match observed frequencies; two models with the same AUC can differ greatly in it.

sections.heading: Collinearity is the biology
sections.body: Nutrients travel together in foods. Automatic selection among correlated nutrients picks one marker of a shared source, not a cause; report how often each is selected across resamples rather than a single set.

sections.heading: The algorithm is rarely the lever
sections.body: In MAQC-II, across more than 30,000 models from 36 teams, performance depended mainly on the endpoint and the team's proficiency, and different algorithms performed similarly. Whether tree ensembles beat penalized linear models is disputed.

sections.heading: More features than samples
sections.body: With more features than samples, an unpenalized least-squares or logistic model is degenerate rather than merely overfit: infinitely many coefficient vectors fit the data exactly. Penalization, dimension reduction or one test per feature are the ways through; the elastic net is the standard choice if one model must be named.

sections.heading: Calibrate the trees
sections.body: Boosted trees often produce miscalibrated probabilities: report the calibration curve, or recalibrate on held-out data, never on training rows.

sections.heading: Probabilities, not just ranks
sections.body: Judge models on calibration as well as discrimination: a well-calibrated model with a lower AUC can be more useful than a miscalibrated one with a higher AUC (Van Calster et al. 2019). Each fit here reports its calibration beside the AUC, the customary headline, and ranks the families on log loss, a strictly proper score that rewards calibrated probabilities.

sections.heading: Avoid stepwise selection
sections.body: Stepwise selection produces unstable variable sets, biased coefficients and intervals with the wrong coverage; prefer prespecification or penalization.

teaching.title: Substitution curves
teaching.question: Which nutrient's calories should replace which, and in what steps?
teaching.one_liner: A substitution curve shows the predicted outcome as calories move from one nutrient to another at fixed total energy.
teaching.why: Energy-adjusted effects are substitutions, so name what replaces what. The curve moves calories from the donor to the recipient through each fitted model, only as far as your data hold people with such diets. Both nutrients must carry energy; grams and servings do not make an isocaloric swap.
teaching.consumer: The substitution stage draws one curve per fitted model family.

options.label: 50 kcal steps
options.consequence: Finer steps; the curve's labeled effect is a 50 kcal swap.

options.label: 100 kcal steps
options.consequence: The curve's labeled effect is swapping 100 kcal from donor to recipient.

options.label: 200 kcal steps
options.consequence: Coarser steps; the curve's labeled effect is a 200 kcal swap.

terms.definition: The nutrient whose calories are taken away in a substitution.
The nutrient that receives those calories, so total energy stays the same.
At the same total energy. A substitution is isocaloric only when both parts are measured in calories.
The range of diets actually present in your data; a curve beyond it is extrapolation, so the curve stops there.
Part of another column's total, such as `fat_sat` within `fat_total`: a partition would count it twice, and a substitution moves it with its total.

sections.heading: Adjusting for energy is not enough
sections.body: Adjusting for total energy does not by itself make a substitution isocaloric. The components must be measured and analyzed in calories; in grams or servings, the substitution reported is not the one intended.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#05 · Compositional structure and substitution modeling

sections.heading: Parts of a whole
sections.body: When shares of energy sum to 100%, one part is determined by the others, and a coefficient on percent energy from fat has no meaning until you say what the fat replaced.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#05 · Compositional structure and substitution modeling

sections.heading: Three legitimate designs
sections.body: A leave-one-out model (every component but one, plus total energy, in kcal), compositional log-ratios, or an explicit difference of coefficients. The first and last are conventions; log-ratios are emerging and less familiar to reviewers.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#05 · Compositional structure and substitution modeling

sections.heading: Validated inputs
sections.body: A review of 100 substitution studies (Louie & Bhowmik 2026) found 53% used unvalidated food-frequency variables; where validation was reported, correlations with reference methods ranged from 0.12 to 0.77.

evidence.source: research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#05 · Compositional structure and substitution modeling
research/NUTRITION_PACK.md#05 · Compositional structure and substitution modeling

teaching.title: Opening the seal
teaching.question: Open the held-out rows and score the models once?
teaching.one_liner: The held-out scores exist but are withheld until now; opening the seal fixes them in the record.
teaching.why: Held-out rows give one honest number only if nothing was tuned against them. Once opened, the scores stay in the record. A later change still refits every model, but its sentence and the manuscript mark it as made after the seal was opened.
teaching.consumer: The Results, the manuscript's performance table and the mark on any later change read it.

options.label: Open the seal
options.consequence: Each model is scored once on the held-out rows; those scores are fixed.

options.label: Keep it sealed
options.consequence: The Results stay on cross-validation; the held-out rows stay unread.

terms.definition: A change made after the held-out scores were seen; the record and the manuscript mark it so.

sections.heading: What to report from the held-out rows
sections.body: Discrimination ranks and calibration measures magnitude; you need both. Report the C-statistic with its interval, the calibration intercept and slope, the calibration curve and the Brier score.

sections.heading: Resample the whole pipeline
sections.body: Internal validation must resample the entire modeling pipeline: imputation, transformation, selection and tuning.

sections.heading: A single split is the weakest
sections.body: Bootstrap optimism correction is the recommended default and repeated cross-validation is acceptable; a single train and test split is the weakest option at typical clinical sample sizes.

models.label: Linear model
models.inductive_bias: Each predictor adds a straight-line effect; effects add up, with no interactions unless you build them.
strengths: Coefficients read as effects per unit, with confidence intervals.
Stable and transparent with many rows per predictor.
cautions: Misses curves and interactions it is not given.
Unstable when predictors are many or strongly correlated.

models.label: Elastic net
models.inductive_bias: Straight-line effects shrunk toward zero; few predictors matter, correlated ones share weight.
strengths: Works with more predictors than rows.
Tunes its own penalty by cross-validation on training rows.
cautions: Shrunk coefficients have no confidence intervals.
Which of several correlated predictors it keeps is arbitrary.

models.label: Boosted trees
models.inductive_bias: Effects are step functions that can bend and interact; many shallow trees each correct the last.
strengths: Finds curves and interactions without being told.
Uses rows with missing values as they are.
cautions: No coefficients: effects are read from curves.
Overfits easily and needs many rows.
Validated by cross-validation: Harrell's bootstrap overstates a near-interpolating learner's performance.

models.label: Feature-wise regression
models.inductive_bias: Each exposure tested on its own with the covariates; Benjamini–Hochberg holds the false-discovery rate.
strengths: Valid tests with more features than rows.
Holds the false-discovery rate across thousands of features (Benjamini–Hochberg).
cautions: Each estimate ignores the other exposures: one separate question per feature.
Tests only: it makes no predictions and has no cross-validated score.
Intervals assume equal residual variance; robust ones fail at the thresholds it tests.

models.label: Proportional-odds model
models.inductive_bias: Each predictor shifts the odds of a higher level by one factor, the same at every cut-point.
strengths: Keeps the order of the levels without assuming they are equally spaced.
Coefficients are cumulative odds ratios, with intervals.
cautions: Assumes one odds ratio at every cut-point (proportional odds); the Brant test checks it.
Misses curves and interactions it is not given.

models.label: Random-intercept mixed model
models.inductive_bias: Straight-line effects, plus a level of its own for each unit whose rows repeat.
strengths: Intervals that allow for a unit's rows being alike, even with few units.
Uses variation within and between units, weighted by how alike a unit's rows are.
cautions: Assumes each unit's own level is unrelated to the predictors; otherwise within- and between-unit effects are blended.
Adds nothing when no unit repeats, and predicts a new unit from its fixed effects alone.

models.label: GEE (exchangeable)
models.inductive_bias: Population-average straight-line or log-odds effects; a unit's rows share one correlation.
strengths: Population-average effects, with intervals robust to how a unit's rows correlate.
Weights rows by their estimated within-unit correlation, which can sharpen estimates.
cautions: Its intervals rest on unit-level residuals, so they are refused below the unit floor.
Adds nothing when no unit repeats, and predicts from population-average effects.

models.label: Cox proportional hazards
models.inductive_bias: Each predictor multiplies the hazard by a constant ratio over all of follow-up; effects add on the log scale.
strengths: Uses every row's follow-up, censored or not, and rows that enter late.
Hazard ratios with intervals; no assumption about the baseline hazard's shape.
cautions: Assumes each hazard ratio is constant over follow-up; a check says when it is not.
Misses curves and interactions it is not given.

models.label: Screened elastic net
models.inductive_bias: Only features with a strong marginal association survive; among them, straight-line effects shrunk toward zero.
strengths: Cuts tens of thousands of features to n / log n before the penalty, inside each fold.
Tunes its penalty by cross-validation on training rows.
cautions: A feature that matters only jointly with others can be screened out.
Which features survive changes from fold to fold.
